::: {.cite-bar .domain-aid-sanctions}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Pub. L. 104-114]{.cite} [110 Stat. 785]{.cite} [22 U.S.C. 6021 et seq.]{.cite}
:::

Wrote the Cuba embargo into statute so that a President cannot lift it alone, and extended its reach to foreign companies that use property confiscated by the Cuban government.

## Key provisions

- Title I: codified the embargo regulations as they stood in 1996.
- Title II: conditions for a transition government that must be met before the embargo can end.
- Title III: a private right of action in U.S. courts against those who traffic in confiscated property.
- Title IV: denial of U.S. visas to executives of trafficking companies.

## Why it matters

It is the leading example of Congress taking a sanctions program out of presidential hands. The embargo it codified was built on the [Trading with the Enemy Act](twea-1917.qmd) and on Section 620(a) of the [Foreign Assistance Act](faa-1961.qmd).

## Current status

In force. Title III lawsuits, suspended by every President for 23 years, have been allowed since May 2019.
